pages.md:
On Windows and Linux, `⌘` is **Ctrl**, `⌥` is **Alt** and `⇧` is
**Shift**; the app shows the right keys for your system.
`⌘/` opens this list inside the app.

Everything Lumen can do is a command in the **command palette** (`⌘K`),
which shows each command's shortcut when it has one.

## Anywhere in the app

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `⌘K` | Command palette |
| `⌘/` | Keyboard shortcuts |
| `⌘N` | New document |
| `⌘O` | Open file |
| `⌘S` | Save |
| `⇧⌘S` | Save as |
| `⌘1` / `⌘2` / `⌘3` / `⌘4` | Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG |
| `⌘H` | Find and replace |
| `⇧⌘V` | Smart Insert (paste anything, detected and wrapped) |
| `⇧⌘F` | Focus mode (press again to leave) |
| `Esc` | Close the open dialog; also stops every running AI request, like `⌘K → AI: Cancel` |
| `⌥⌘D` | Today's note ([daily notes](/workspace/hebrew-calendar/)) |
| `⌘Z` outside an editor | Restore the last deleted file or folder ([undoing a delete](/workspace/history/#undoing-a-delete)) |

Workspace search has no global key of its own today: open it with
`⌘K → Search workspace…`. Printing is `⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`; `⌘P`
opens the browser's own print dialog.

## In the editor

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `⌘Z` / `⇧⌘Z` | Undo / redo |
| `⌘F` | Find in this note (source editor) |
| `⇧⌥F` | Format the document |
| `Ctrl+Space` | Ask the AI for a continuation (ghost text) |

## In the tab strip and the rich editor

| Keys | Where | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `⌘W` | a focused tab | Close it |
| `↑` / `↓` | a focused block handle | Move the block up / down |
| `Enter` / `Space` | a focused block handle | Put the cursor at the block's start |

pages.title: Welcome to Lumen
pages.description: Why we built Lumen, and what makes it different from Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear.
pages.md:
## Where Lumen fits

There's no shortage of markdown editors — Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear,
Logseq, Roam, HackMD, Joplin, Craft. Lumen sits at a specific intersection:

| | Lumen | Obsidian | Notion | Typora | Bear |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Local-first (works offline) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Web app (no install) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Auto data → table + chart | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ DB only | ❌ | ❌ |
| RTL / Hebrew first-class | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ |
| Mermaid + Graphviz + PlantUML + ABC + 3D | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ Mermaid only | ⚠️ | ❌ |
| Real-time collab | ✅ WebRTC | ❌ | ✅ Pro | ❌ | ❌ |
| Smart search (embeddings) | ✅ Pro | ⚠️ plugin | ✅ AI | ❌ | ❌ |
| MCP for AI agents | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Local LLM (WebGPU) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Open source (MIT) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

## What we believe

**1. Plain text wins.** Lumen never invents a proprietary format — every
note is portable markdown. Rendering is opinionated; storage isn't.

**2. Data is content.** A spreadsheet inside a note shouldn't need a
plugin. Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and it just becomes a table with
chart suggestions.

**3. AI assists, never gates.** Bring your own key. Disable AI entirely
and Lumen still ships every other feature.

**4. Privacy is structural, not promised.** Local-first storage, transport-encrypted
(WebRTC DTLS) collab, opt-in telemetry that's off by default.

Continue to the [Quickstart](/getting-started/quickstart/) →

pages.title: What's new
pages.description: After an update, Lumen shows that version's release notes once, in your interface language.
pages.md:
When Lumen updates, the next time you open it you see **What's new**: that
version's release notes, in the language of your interface. They appear
**once per version**. A new install doesn't show them, since nothing is new
to you yet.

To read them again at any time, run `⌘K → "What's new in this version"`.

The notes ship inside the app, so they work offline.

## For maintainers: where the notes come from

- **English** is `CHANGELOG.md`, which `node scripts/release.mjs prepare`
  writes from the commit subjects (see `RELEASE.md`). Commit links and
  scopes are left out of what readers see.
- **Other languages** live in `changelog/<locale>.md`, for example
  `changelog/he.md`, with the same `## [x.y.z] - date` sections.
  `release.mjs prepare` copies each new English section into every file
  there, marked `<!-- untranslated -->`.
- To translate a release, translate the section and delete that line.
  Until then the app shows the English notes under the language's own
  headings, and says they aren't translated yet.

## Account

- [Organization settings](/account/organization/) — Name your organization, restrict e-mail domains, check SSO and members.
- [Signing in](/account/sign-in/) — What each sign-in status means and how to fix the common errors.
- [Single sign-on (SSO)](/account/sso/) — Sign in with your company's identity provider through WorkOS.

## AI

- [Auto-tag + link suggestions](/ai/agents/) — AI assistants that read your workspace and propose structure.
- [AI-written text](/ai/authorship/) — Text the AI wrote is shown lighter until you edit it — in the editor, saved per note, and optionally in the export.
- [Local autocomplete (FIM)](/ai/autocomplete/) — Completions as you type from a coding model on this device — Ollama with qwen2.5-coder, or the in-browser model — with no cloud route at all.
- [Batch jobs — pause, resume, progress](/ai/batch/) — Run tags, summaries or translations over a folder on this device, watch the progress live, and pause, resume or cancel the job — also after a reload.
- [AI cost — usage meter and answer cache](/ai/cost/) — See what your AI requests cost, and avoid paying twice for the same answer.
- [Data analyst](/ai/data-analyst/) — Ask a question about a table in your note; a short Python program answers it on this device, checked by a second run.
- [DictaLM 3.0 (Hebrew)](/ai/dictalm3/) — Dicta's Hebrew–English model in the local model catalogue — what is verified, what waits for a check, and when it may become the default.
- [AI doctor](/ai/doctor/) — One check of the whole local-AI stack, from Ollama to the on-device engines, with the exact fix for each row.
- [Choosing the Hebrew search model](/ai/embedding-competition/) — How Lumen picks the model behind semantic search and suggested links. It runs a competition on a hard Hebrew question set, and the default changes only for a clear, measured gain.
- [External OCR benchmark (HebOCRBench)](/ai/hebocrbench/) — How Lumen's OCR is measured on HebOCRBench, an outside Hebrew benchmark whose answers only its organisers hold, and where the scores are published.
- [Hebrew dictation, models and accuracy](/ai/hebrew-dictation/) — Which speech model Lumen uses for Hebrew in the browser and on phones, how each sentence is re-read by Whisper, and how accuracy (WER) is measured.
- [Image descriptions on this device](/ai/image-captions/) — Alt text for pasted and attached images — OCR, a local vision model, or a captioning model in the browser. Nothing is sent to the cloud.
- [Image search by description](/ai/image-search/) — Find an image in your notes by describing it, in Hebrew or English, on this device.
- [Train a model on your style, on this machine](/ai/local-fine-tune/) — A LoRA adapter trained on your own notes on a Mac or NVIDIA computer and used in Ollama. Nothing is uploaded.
- [Local LLM (web-llm + WebGPU)](/ai/local-llm/) — Run AI prompts entirely on your device — private, offline-capable, no per-token cost.
- [Meeting notes on this device](/ai/meeting-notes/) — Record a meeting, transcribe it on this device, and get its decisions, tasks with owner and date, and open questions — tasks in the task panel, dates in a calendar file.
- [Meeting transcripts with speakers](/ai/meeting-speakers/) — Transcribe a meeting recording on this device with who said what, name each speaker once, and get the meeting notes on top.
- [Model credits](/ai/model-credits/) — Where Lumen credits the models it ships or downloads, ivrit.ai and Dicta first, with each licence's requirements.
- [Models day on a free cloud GPU](/ai/models-cloud/) — One command runs the real models day, held-out sets included, on a free Kaggle GPU and brings back the signed report. Tal's Mac is only the backup.
- [Hebrew niqqud on this device](/ai/nikud/) — Add or remove vowel points (niqqud) in Hebrew text with a model that runs in your browser.
- [On-device OCR (Hebrew, English, columns)](/ai/ocr/) — How Lumen reads text from images and scanned PDF pages on your device — Latin words inside Hebrew lines, multi-column pages, and the reading order of the result.
- [Organize the vault](/ai/organizer/) — Missing links, tags, duplicates to merge and maps of content for your whole vault — each one a change you approve, with its confidence, reason and a quote.
- [Personal data before the cloud](/ai/pii-redaction/) — When your AI policy lets a request leave this device, Lumen hides e-mails, phone numbers, ID numbers, cards, IBANs, plates and birth dates on the device first, and puts them back in the answer.
- [Read aloud (Hebrew included)](/ai/read-aloud/) — Listen to a note on this device — the word being read is highlighted, the position is kept, and you choose the speed and voice.
- [Search reranking — measured](/ai/reranker/) — What the search reranker adds on Lumen's retrieval golden set, the decision that follows, and how to measure the model yourself.
- [Screenshot to note](/ai/screenshot-note/) — Turn a screenshot into Markdown you can edit — tables, lists, code and error messages — with a vision model on your own computer.
- [Speculative decoding in Ollama](/ai/speculative-decoding/) — Ollama 0.34 speeds up some models by guessing several tokens at once. Lumen measures it per model, keeps it only where it helps, and turns it off for reproducible evals.
- [English spelling on this device](/ai/spelling/) — Spell-check English notes with a dictionary that ships with Lumen — no LanguageTool account, no request leaves the device.
- [Structured output and Chrome's built-in model](/ai/structured-output/) — How Lumen's local AI returns JSON that always matches what the feature asked for, on Ollama, the in-browser model or Chrome's built-in model — and when the built-in model is used with no download.
- [Local translation](/ai/translation/) — Translate a document on this device, in three layers — Chrome's built-in translator, Opus-MT for Hebrew ⇄ English, M2M100 for the rest — with code and links kept exactly.
- [Voice commands, on this device](/ai/voice-commands/) — Say "new note", "search…" or "add task…" in Hebrew or English. Lumen recognises the speech and the command locally, and asks before anything that deletes.
- [Hebrew Whisper on the desktop](/ai/whisper-desktop/) — Transcribe long Hebrew recordings on your computer with ivrit.ai's Whisper in whisper.cpp — one sentence per line, each time a link into the audio.

## Blocks

- [Math inside Hebrew text](/blocks/math-in-hebrew/) — Formulas in a right-to-left sentence keep their order in the editor, the preview, PDF and Word.
- [Sheet block](/blocks/sheet/) — A small spreadsheet inside a note, stored as CSV, with A1 formulas on the app's formula engine.

## Collaboration

- [Encrypted live sharing](/collab/e2ee-sharing/) — Share a note live through a server that stores and relays only ciphertext, names and cursors included.
- [End-to-end encryption for collab](/collab/encryption/) — Add a room password and no relay, signaling server or sync server can read your document.
- [Live canvas](/collab/live-canvas/) — Draw on one canvas together during a collab session — edits and pointers appear as they happen, over the same encrypted room as the note.
- [The public server](/collab/public-server/) — A free live-share server for everyone that stores only encrypted rooms, deletes idle rooms after 90 days and keeps no IP addresses in its logs.
- [Encrypted share link](/collab/share-link/) — Share a read-only copy of one note as a link that carries the note itself, encrypted. No server, no account.
- [Sharing, roles and comment threads](/collab/sharing/) — Share a note to view, comment or edit with a link that expires; revoke it; comment threads with mentions.
- [Suggestions and named versions](/collab/suggestions-versions/) — Suggest edits that change nothing until someone accepts them, accept or reject one person's suggestions at a time, see who wrote what (the AI included), and name versions to compare word by word.
- [Real-time WebRTC collaboration](/collab/webrtc/) — Multi-cursor editing over a peer-to-peer mesh — no server account, no central log of your doc.

## Contributing

- [Budgets that only go down](/contributing/budgets/) — The bundle budgets and the performance gate's FCP and LCP limits are lowered after every train to what the train measured plus 2 %, and never raised. Exceptions carry an expiry date and fail once it has passed.
- [Checks on every branch (Vercel)](/contributing/checks/) — Lumen's gates run in the Vercel build of every branch, without GitHub Actions — what runs, what a red status means, and where the old CI checks went.
- [Code checks: strings, coverage, vault backends](/contributing/code-checks/) — Three checks a contributor meets in the code itself — no user-visible string outside t(), test coverage over all of src/, and one contract suite every vault backend passes.
- [Design system](/contributing/design-system/) — Lumen's tokens for colour, space, radius, type, elevation and motion, the rules the code is held to, and the shared components.
- [The open Hebrew voice (recording kit)](/contributing/hebrew-voice/) — How to record, check and train the first neural Hebrew voice released as CC0, so read-aloud in Hebrew is open to every app.
- [Independent review](/contributing/independent-review/) — Every change to a sensitive path needs a review receipt for its head commit from a reviewer that did not write it, with attack tests, before it is merged — integration trains included.
- [Compiling the native code offline](/contributing/native-check/) — How Lumen's Rust, Java and Swift code is compiled without crates.io, the Android SDK or Xcode — what the check proves, what it cannot, and what still needs a Mac.
- [Nightly runs and receipts](/contributing/nightly/) — npm run nightly runs the flake hunt, the perf checks, the review triage and the weekly health on your own machine, and writes a signed report for each, without GitHub Actions.
- [The PR check](/contributing/pr-check/) — npm run pr:check is the local PR gate that replaces Danger.js and size-limit. It reports bundle size against the base, PR body sections, [skip ci] commits, unregistered network calls, licences and the domain rule.
- [Before main, WebKit and Safari](/contributing/promotion/) — npm run promote:check refuses to promote main to a commit without a signed WebKit receipt and a signed Safari receipt for that commit. WebKit runs on the verification factory, real Safari on BrowserStack's open-source plan.
- [Nightly redaction fuzz](/contributing/redaction-fuzz/) — Every night the second host feeds 20,000 generated notes to the preview and the export, and any passage the preview shades but the export keeps becomes a permanent test.
- [Second maintainer](/contributing/second-maintainer/) — Onboarding for Lumen's second maintainer — access, the local checks, how to review a sensitive change and add the human-reviewed label, security reports, and what only the owner holds today.
- [Skipped tests](/contributing/skipped-tests/) — Every skipped test says why, for which task and until when; npm run hygiene fails on one that does not, and npm run skips lists them all.
- [Every PR on the train head](/contributing/train-base/) — A pull request is based on the current train or on main, never on another PR's branch. pr:check fails a stacked base and a stack deeper than 1, warns about an older train and about drift, and fails an old merge base or a criss-cross. scripts/restack.mjs prints how to move a stacked PR onto the train.
- [The weekly train](/contributing/train/) — How Lumen's integration trains are built, checked and promoted, every week. npm run train:build merges the PRs and resolves what it can, npm run train:status shows the ledger and the gates, and main moves at least once a week.
- [Translation drafts](/contributing/translation-drafts/) — npm run i18n:draft drafts new UI strings in all seven languages with a local model; drafts stay "needs review" until a person approves them.
- [Languages in beta, and how to help](/contributing/translations/) — English and Hebrew are Lumen's full languages; the other six were translated by machine and are marked Beta (machine translation, awaiting native review). How to report a translation issue from inside the app.
- [Visual regression](/contributing/visual-regression/) — npm run test:visual compares ten surfaces in English and Hebrew, light and dark, with their pixel baselines — locally, no CI needed.
- [Translating on Weblate](/contributing/weblate/) — Review and fix Lumen's six machine-translated languages on Hosted Weblate, in the browser, with every change coming back to the repository as a pull request.

## Editor

- [Accessibility](/editor/accessibility/) — Keyboard use, screen readers, contrast and reduced motion in Lumen — and how each is checked.
- [Arabic (beta)](/editor/arabic/) — Write Arabic next to Hebrew and English in one note. Each line takes its own direction, tashkeel can be hidden or removed, search ignores it, and Arabic spelling runs on this device.
- [Direction marks (bidi)](/editor/direction-marks/) — See the invisible characters that set text direction, clean the ones that do nothing, fix reversed brackets, and catch Trojan Source text.
- [Handwriting and ink](/editor/handwriting/) — Write or draw with a pen, an Apple Pencil, a finger or a mouse inside a note. The ink is saved as SVG in the Markdown file, so the note still opens in Obsidian and other editors.
- [Hebrew dictionary and synonyms](/editor/hebrew-dictionary/) — Definitions, synonyms and the niqqud of a word, from Hebrew Wiktionary, offline inside the editor.
- [Hebrew grammar and style](/editor/hebrew-grammar/) — Hebrew grammar and style checks that run on this device, beyond spelling, with three writing levels and a short explanation for each suggestion.
- [Hebrew typography](/editor/hebrew-typography/) — Gershayim, geresh, maqaf, Hebrew quotation marks and numbers, fixed as you type or for a whole note. Each rule can be turned off.
- [Hebrew and right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/) — Writing in Hebrew (and Arabic) in Lumen — direction per line, the interface in Hebrew, search that ignores niqqud and prefixes, spelling on this device, and exports that keep the direction.

sections.heading: Contributing
sections.text: Budgets that only go down — The bundle budgets and the performance gate's FCP and LCP limits are lowered after every train to what the train measured plus 2 %, and never raised. Checks on every branch (Vercel) — Lumen's gates run in the Vercel build of every branch, without GitHub Actions — what runs, what a red status means, and where the old CI checks went. Code checks: strings, coverage, vault backends — Three checks a contributor meets in the code itself — no user-visible string outside t(), test coverage over all of src/, and one contract suite every vault backend passes. Design system — Lumen's tokens for colour, space, radius, type, elevation and motion, the rules the code is held to, and the shared components. The open Hebrew voice (recording kit) — How to record, check and train the first neural Hebrew voice released as CC0, so read-aloud in Hebrew is open to every app. Independent review — Every change to a sensitive path needs a review receipt for its head commit from a reviewer that did not write it, with attack tests, before it is merged — integration trains included. Compiling the native code offline — How Lumen's Rust, Java and Swift code is compiled without crates.io, the Android SDK or Xcode — what the check proves, what it cannot, and what still needs a Mac. Nightly runs and receipts — npm run nightly runs the flake hunt, the perf checks, the review triage and the weekly health on your own machine, and writes a signed report for each, without GitHub Actions. The PR check — npm run pr:check is the local PR gate that replaces Danger.js and size-limit. It reports bundle size against the base, PR body sections, [skip ci] commits, unregistered network calls, licences and the domain rule. Before main, WebKit and Safari — npm run promote:check refuses to promote main to a commit without a signed WebKit receipt and a signed Safari receipt for that commit. WebKit runs on the verification factory, real Safari on BrowserStack's open-source plan. Nightly redaction fuzz — Every night the second host feeds 20,000 generated notes to the preview and the export, and any passage the preview shades but the export keeps becomes a permanent test. Second maintainer — Onboarding for Lumen's second maintainer — access, the local checks, how to review a sensitive change and add the human-reviewed label, security reports, and what only the owner holds today. Skipped tests — Every skipped test says why, for which task and until when; npm run hygiene fails on one that does not, and npm run skips lists them all. Every PR on the train head — A pull request is based on the current train or on main, never on another PR's branch. pr:check fails a stacked base and a stack deeper than 1, warns about an older train and about drift, and fails an old merge base or a criss-cross. scripts/restack.mjs prints how to move a stacked PR onto the train. The weekly train — How Lumen's integration trains are built, checked and promoted, every week. npm run train:build merges the PRs and resolves what it can, npm run train:status shows the ledger and the gates, and main moves at least once a week. Translation drafts — npm run i18n:draft drafts new UI strings in all seven languages with a local model; drafts stay "needs review" until a person approves them. Languages in beta, and how to help — English and Hebrew are Lumen's full languages; the other six were translated by machine and are marked Beta (machine translation, awaiting native review). How to report a translation issue from inside the app. Visual regression — npm run test:visual compares ten surfaces in English and Hebrew, light and dark, with their pixel baselines — locally, no CI needed. Translating on Weblate — Review and fix Lumen's six machine-translated languages on Hosted Weblate, in the browser, with every change coming back to the repository as a pull request.

sections.heading: Editor
sections.text: Accessibility — Keyboard use, screen readers, contrast and reduced motion in Lumen — and how each is checked. Arabic (beta) — Write Arabic next to Hebrew and English in one note. Each line takes its own direction, tashkeel can be hidden or removed, search ignores it, and Arabic spelling runs on this device. Direction marks (bidi) — See the invisible characters that set text direction, clean the ones that do nothing, fix reversed brackets, and catch Trojan Source text. Handwriting and ink — Write or draw with a pen, an Apple Pencil, a finger or a mouse inside a note. The ink is saved as SVG in the Markdown file, so the note still opens in Obsidian and other editors. Hebrew dictionary and synonyms — Definitions, synonyms and the niqqud of a word, from Hebrew Wiktionary, offline inside the editor. Hebrew grammar and style — Hebrew grammar and style checks that run on this device, beyond spelling, with three writing levels and a short explanation for each suggestion. Hebrew typography — Gershayim, geresh, maqaf, Hebrew quotation marks and numbers, fixed as you type or for a whole note. Each rule can be turned off. Hebrew and right-to-left — Writing in Hebrew (and Arabic) in Lumen — direction per line, the interface in Hebrew, search that ignores niqqud and prefixes, spelling on this device, and exports that keep the direction. Images, attachments, copy and backlinks — Resize an image by dragging, reset it with a double-click, delete a note's own attachments with it, copy as formatted text, and search the backlinks. Legal citations (Israel) — Rulings, laws, bills, books and articles by the Israeli uniform citation rules, and a citation from a case number in the note. Markdown fidelity — How closely Lumen follows the CommonMark and GFM specs, and the promise that opening and saving a file in either editor gives you back the same bytes. Messages, empty states and undo — How Lumen talks when something fails, when a panel is empty, and before it deletes anything — and the guide for writing those messages. Editor modes — Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG — pick the one that fits the task. Outline mode and block operations — Fold headings and lists, zoom into one block, and move, indent, duplicate or delete whole blocks — on a plain Markdown file, in both editors. Pasting from Word, Google Docs and the web — Paste from Word, Google Docs, Wikipedia, news sites or Gmail, in Hebrew or English, and get clean Markdown that keeps the structure and drops the styling. Hebrew pasted from a PDF — Hebrew copied out of a PDF often comes out backwards or with the wrong final letters. Lumen notices and offers the fix. Reading aids — Niqqud for reading that never changes the note, a dyslexia-friendly layout, and read-aloud that highlights each word. Reading views — Source, preview and outline side by side with linked scrolling, and the keyboard between the columns. Screen reader protocol — The fixed Hebrew journey run with NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack before a release, and its results. Testing with screen reader users — The kit for sessions with three Hebrew screen reader users — who to ask, the invitation, consent, the tasks, how a session is scored, and what happens to each barrier. Smart Insert (⌘⇧V) — Paste anything into one dialog — Lumen detects the type and wraps it in the right block. Themes and CSS snippets — Five built-in themes, among them one for Hebrew reading, theme files on the documented tokens, and CSS snippets from the vault that can never reach the network. Writing tools — Theme settings, voice memos and dictation, the canvas, sync conflicts and the app's dialogs. Touch and phones — Using Lumen with a finger or a pen — dragging, touch targets, the notch and the outline sheet — and how each is tested. Widgets, Shortcuts and Siri — A Lumen widget on the home screen, Siri and Spotlight on iPhone, App Shortcuts on Android, and "Add to inbox" from the Shortcuts app — plus the steps to build them. Yiddish and Ladino — Write Yiddish in YIVO spelling and Ladino in Latin or Hebrew letters — language tags, direction, spelling, and transliteration both ways, on this device.

sections.heading: Getting started
sections.text: Beta channel and feature flags — Try new features before everyone else, on the web or in the desktop app, and turn any beta feature on or off on your own device. The desktop app — Windows, tabs you drag between them, the tray with quick capture, opening .md files from Finder or Explorer, and lumen:// links. Desktop app updates — How the Lumen desktop app checks for, verifies and installs updates, and what it sends. Send feedback — Report a bug, an idea or a question as a GitHub issue or as text to copy. Lumen has no feedback server, and nothing is sent until you click. Moving from Bear — Export Bear notes as Markdown and bring them, with their images, into Lumen. Moving from Evernote — Get your notebooks out of Evernote and into Lumen as Markdown, with their images and attachments. Moving from Google Docs — Turn Google Docs into Markdown notes in Lumen — one document, or a whole Drive folder. Moving from Notion — Export a Notion workspace and bring its pages, links and attachments into Lumen. Moving from Obsidian — Bring an Obsidian vault into Lumen — notes, attachments, links and Bases — and what changes on the way. Install with a package manager — Install the Lumen desktop app with Homebrew, winget, Flatpak or the AUR, and where those packages come from. Install Lumen — Lumen in the browser, as an installed web app, on the desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) and on iOS / Android — and what each one stores where. Leaving Evernote or Notion? — How to take your notes out of Evernote, Notion, Apple Notes, Google Keep, OneNote or Obsidian, and bring them into Lumen in one step, with one click to take it back. Quickstart — Get to your first beautiful Lumen document in 60 seconds. Welcome to Lumen — Why we built Lumen, and what makes it different from Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear.

sections.heading: Plugins
sections.text: Developing a plugin — Scaffold a sandboxed plugin with create-lumen-plugin, run it with hot reload in developer mode, test it in Node with the test kit, and see what it does in the Developer panel. Plugin registry and the built-in ten — The ten plugins in Lumen's plugin gallery, what each one may do, and how the static registry is built and scanned. Plugin sandbox and permissions — How Lumen runs plugins with no access by default — QuickJS for logic, UI as data, a capability list the user grants. Plugin signing keys — Decide which publishers' plugins Lumen trusts. Templates — Start a note from a template — the built-in ones, the gallery, and the ones you install — and where an installed template lives.

sections.heading: Project
sections.text: The beta programme — Join the beta from inside Lumen, send feedback as a prefilled GitHub issue, and — only if you ask — a weekly report of counts. Nothing leaves without your click. Hebrew in notes, measured — Lumen on public Hebrew benchmarks — bidi, dictation, niqqud, handwriting — next to Obsidian, Notion and Apple Notes where they were measured too. Issue triage — How new GitHub issues are labelled, checked for duplicates and linked to the plan within 24 hours. Owner session command — One command per owner session. It prints exactly what to do in the browser, runs the commands for you after asking, verifies the result through the APIs, records a signed receipt per step and resumes where you stopped. Owner sessions — Everything only the owner can do — accounts, GPU runs, golden data, devices — in three sittings ordered by dependency, with the time and the exact command for each, and free cloud devices instead of owning test phones. Open PR triage — One decision table for every open pull request — in main, in a train, superseded, dependabot, or still needed — and the commands that close each category with a comment. Releasing a version — One local command builds, signs and checks a release, and with --publish puts it on GitHub Releases with signed desktop updates. No GitHub Actions. Usability tests with Hebrew speakers — How Lumen is tested with people who write in Hebrew — the ten tasks, SUS, the consent-first session recorder that keeps no note text, and the analysis.

sections.heading: Security and privacy
sections.text: Allowed image hosts — See which sites may always load images in your notes, and revoke one or all of them. Monitoring and web vitals — Error reports are off by default and sent only with your consent; web vitals never leave your device. Mutation testing — How Lumen checks that the tests of its security-critical code, such as encryption, the keyring, sync merges and the privacy ledger, really catch bugs. Photo metadata — Photos you paste or drop into a note lose their GPS position, time, device and text metadata before they are stored. The e2e test surface — window. lumen.agentReview exists only in development and tests. Trusted repositories — Let agents propose changes in a git repository you own without the extra outside-content question. Usage on this device — Lumen counts starts, commands and errors on your device only. The weekly report is off until you turn it on, and you send it yourself. Nothing leaves without your click. Vault encryption at rest — Encrypt the whole vault where it is stored — OPFS, a real folder or the desktop folder — with a passphrase, a recovery key and auto-lock. Secrets and encryption — How Lumen stores API keys and tokens, and how to encrypt a document.

sections.heading: Self-hosting
sections.text: CI on Buildkite, without GitHub Actions — Buildkite Free schedules lumen-md's gates on our own machines (the verification factory's host and a Mac) and posts a commit status for every gate on every PR, plus a signed receipt. Moving production to another host — The runbook for moving Lumen's production from Vercel Hobby to Cloudflare Pages in under an hour, before the first payment. It covers the new address, the users' notes that stay with the old one, the redirect, the checks and the way back. Self-hosting with Docker — Run Lumen on your own infrastructure with the docker-compose bundle. Where Lumen runs — What works on which host — Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel and the Docker image — and how each one is configured. Android and iOS builds — How the Android APK and iOS IPA are built on every pull request, what is unsigned until the store accounts exist, and which secrets sign them. Native builds on free hosts — How the desktop app, the Android AAB and the iOS IPA are really compiled without GitHub Actions — a Linux script for the second host, Codemagic's free macOS minutes, and a robo run on Firebase Test Lab or BrowserStack. Performance gate — npm run perf:gate measures FCP, LCP, TBT, TTI and CLS of a production build in Chromium, on desktop and a throttled phone, and fails on the error thresholds, without GitHub Actions. A second host and tests without Vercel — Why Cloudflare Pages is Lumen's second host next to Vercel Hobby, what each free tier allows, how to deploy the same build there, what to do when a quota runs out, and how to run the whole test pipeline in Docker. The verification factory — A free second machine that runs every test of every verify/ head each night in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, signs a receipt per commit and posts the result to GitHub as commit statuses, without GitHub Actions.

sections.heading: Sync and publishing
sections.text: Private classroom — A teacher hands out a template, students hand in sealed work, and the teacher's comments come back. Only the teacher reads a student's work, and the server reads nothing. Sync providers — Where the encrypted vault can live — WebDAV, S3-compatible storage, Dropbox, Google Drive — how to connect each, what each server must support, and how notes from the old plain-text sync are moved into the vault. Keys, rotation and revocation — Argon2id, age interop, key rotation without re-uploading, removing a lost device, and the public protocol spec. Encrypted sync (E2EE) — The end-to-end encrypted sync protocol — what is encrypted, what the sync service sees, rollback protection and its trust-on-first-use limit. Git sync — Clone, pull and push a git repository from Lumen — safely. A pull merges, never deletes, and never overwrites a note you are editing. Sync on the local network — Sync two devices directly over your own network, end-to-end encrypted, with no cloud and no internet. Automatic merging — When the same note changed in two places, Lumen merges the two edits itself and asks only when both changed the same words — the same way for encrypted sync, git and edits made outside Lumen. Publish to your own site — Turn the notes you pick into a website with navigation, search and right-to-left pages, on your own GitHub Pages or as a .zip for any static host. Read-mode publishing — Publishing a note as a read-only web page — what exists today, the server it needs, and what is not built yet. Real servers and conditional writes — Which WebDAV and S3 servers keep compare-and-swap, measured against the real servers, and how to run the same check against yours. The share servers on Cloudflare — Deploy the live-share server and the encrypted sync relay to Cloudflare Workers with one command, then check the delay, the limits and that no note text is kept. Family and classroom vaults (roles) — One encrypted vault shared by a family or a class, with reader, writer and admin roles, and no accounts. The relay accepts a change only with a writer's signature. Publish to Bluesky and the fediverse — Publish a note as a Standard.site document in your own AT Protocol account, so Bluesky shows it with a rich preview, readers like Leaflet show it in full, and Bridgy Fed can bring it to Mastodon.

sections.heading: Workspace
sections.text: Israeli academic calendar — Semesters, Moed A and Moed B, breaks and make-up days of your institution in the daily note, and the year as an ICS file. Backups to a second drive — A daily backup of the whole vault to another drive or folder, plain or encrypted with age, kept 7 days, 4 weeks and 6 months, and a restore you can check. Ben-Yehuda library (offline) — Download the public-domain works of Project Ben-Yehuda once, then search, read, quote and highlight Hebrew literature with no network. Writing a book — Chapters as notes in order, word goals per chapter and per book, today's words and a streak, and the book assembled into a Hebrew EPUB 3 and a print-ready PDF. Calendar sync (CalDAV and ICS) — Keep the vault's dated tasks in sync with a CalDAV calendar (Fastmail, Nextcloud, iCloud), and see subscribed calendars' events in the daily note. Note cards and image export — Put vault notes on the canvas as live cards, edit them in place, and export the canvas as PNG, SVG or PDF with Hebrew intact. Diagrams on the canvas (Mermaid and "draw me") — Turn Mermaid into shapes you can edit on the canvas, or describe a diagram and let a model on this device draw it. Canvas (Excalidraw) — The whiteboard — on Excalidraw, saved as open .excalidraw files in your vault, fully on your device — and what happens to your old tldraw canvases. WhatsApp and Telegram chats into notes — Import an exported WhatsApp or Telegram chat into notes, one per day or one per chat, with its media, entirely on this device. Contacts (vCard) — Import a .vcf from your phone or Google into person notes, merge it with people already in the vault, and export people back as vCard 4.0. Database views — Editable Table / Cards / Kanban / List / Calendar views over your YAML frontmatter. Vault Doctor — Find broken links, orphans and near-duplicate notes across the workspace, without AI. Embedded queries and saved searches — A dataview block runs common Obsidian Dataview queries, and saved searches sit in the sidebar. All of them update as the vault changes. Entity graph — People, places, organisations, events, laws, sources and concepts found in your notes, each relation backed by an exact quote from a paragraph, reviewed by you before anything is written. EPUB reader and reading mode — Read EPUB books in the vault (Hebrew right-to-left included), highlight them like PDFs, and read clipped pages in a calm reading mode. Export and import — Take the whole vault out as a .zip or a folder, bring in an Obsidian vault or a Notion export, and convert single files to and from many formats. Notebooks, data files and maps — Jupyter notebooks, CSV/TSV/JSON/YAML/XLSX files and GeoJSON/GPX tracks open in a viewer of their own, without converting them. Text formats: what survives a round trip — Measured results for Markdown → Org, AsciiDoc, LaTeX, OPML, RST and Jupyter → Markdown on the 652 CommonMark spec examples and 50 Hebrew notes. Government data (data.gov.il, CBS) — Put a table or a chart of open government data in a note. The rows are kept as a CSV in your vault, the attribution is written for you, and a refresh shows what changed. Graph and local graph — The knowledge graph of the whole vault — 10,000 notes and 50,000 links — and the local graph of the open note, with filters, colour groups and full keyboard use. Daily notes and the Hebrew calendar — The calendar's holidays, fasts and weekly Torah portion, for Israel or the diaspora, and the {{holiday}} and {{parasha}} placeholders of the daily note. Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero) — Bring your highlights from Kindle, Kobo, Readwise and Zotero into the vault, one note per book, with no duplicates when you import again. Import from other apps — Bring notes from Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Apple Notes, Google Keep, Logseq or OneNote — into a new folder, with a report, undone in one click. JSON Canvas (Obsidian .canvas) — Open Obsidian canvases in Lumen's Excalidraw canvas and write them back as .canvas files. JSON Canvas is an open, MIT-licensed format. Laws and Knesset records — Cite a law by its name, a bill and a committee protocol from the Knesset's open data, keep laws for offline use, and ask the laws you saved. Large vaults and long notes — How Lumen stays fast with 10,000 notes and with a single 2 MB note — and how that is measured. Academic LaTeX export (Hebrew) — Export a note as a LaTeX project — Hebrew right to left with babel, math, Pandoc-style [@key] citations from the vault's BibTeX, and images — that compiles with LuaLaTeX or XeLaTeX. Links, embeds and block references — Link notes with [ and its completion, preview a link by hovering, turn plain mentions into links, embed a note or one of its sections, and link to a single paragraph with ^id. [Audio and video with a transcript — Embed a recording, read its WebVTT or SRT transcript beside the player, and click a line to jump there. The vault in a folder on your phone — In the iOS and Android apps, keep the vault in a real folder — the Files app on iOS, a folder you pick on Android — and see edits made there. Obsidian Bases (.base files) — Open, embed and edit Obsidian Bases files — what is supported, what is not, and how the golden set is checked. Side panels — The file tree, outline, backlinks, tags, comments, trash and version history — what each side panel shows and how to use it. Note properties — The note's front matter as typed fields — text, number, date, list, checkbox and link — where an edit changes only that value. Quick capture (inbox) — Add a thought, task or link to inbox.md in two steps, from the keyboard, the home screen or the share sheet. Reading list — Sources (books, articles, sites) with a reading status, progress that the PDF and EPUB readers keep up to date, and a kanban by status. Related notes while writing — The notes closest to the paragraph you are writing, and the notes it mentions without a link — on this device, without slowing typing. Daily review (spaced repetition) — Review your highlights and question::answer cards a few minutes a day, scheduled by FSRS, with everything kept in the vault. Search operators and #tags — Narrow a search with tag:, path:, "phrases", /regex/ and -exclusions; tags written in the text count like front-matter tags. Workspace search (BM25 + Smart) — Fast keyword search by default, semantic embeddings on demand. Slides from notes and the canvas — Present a note or a canvas as slides, right to left when it's Hebrew, with speaker notes, a presenter view on a second screen, and PDF export. Tasks across the vault — Checklist items with dates and priorities in any note, gathered by queries, a Today panel and reminders. Same syntax as the Obsidian Tasks plugin. Typst export (Hebrew) — Export a note as Typst source that typesets Hebrew right to left, and compile it to PDF with typst. Very large vaults — How Lumen stays fast with 100,000 notes. The search index holds one copy of the text, is kept between sessions, and is updated one note at a time, and big embedding indexes are stored compactly. Your vault in a folder — Keep your notes in a real folder on your computer, in the browser or the desktop app, move them there and back without losing a byte, and see changes other programs make. Voice notes into the inbox — Record a voice note from the capture box; it is transcribed on this device and added to inbox.md, with the recording attached if you want.

## What makes Lumen different


  
    Your notes live in your browser's OPFS. Sync with Git, Dropbox, or your own
    server. Or don't sync at all — Lumen works fully offline.
  
  
    Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and Lumen suggests the right chart with one
    click. Live data via `src=` URLs that auto-refresh.
  
  
    Mermaid · Graphviz · PlantUML · KaTeX · ABC notation · model-viewer ·
    Leaflet maps · ECharts. All first-class.
  
  
    Hebrew and Arabic flow right-to-left throughout the UI. Code blocks, math,
    and the editor stay LTR.
  
  
    Smart search, auto-tagging, link suggestions. Bring your OpenAI key, or
    flip to local LLM (web-llm + WebGPU) — your prompts never leave your
    machine.
  
  
    Lumen ships an MCP server so Claude Desktop / Cursor can read, write, and
    search your workspace through `npx @lumen-md/mcp-server`.
  


## Three lines to get going

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md && npm ci && npm run dev
# open http://localhost:5173
```

Or just visit [lumen.app](https://lumen.app) and start typing — there's
nothing to install.

pages.description: Every method of the lumen object in apiVersion 1, generated from the types, with its capability and a tested example.
pages.md:
<!-- Generated by scripts/plugin-api-docs.mjs — do not edit by hand. -->

This page is generated from `src/plugins/runtime/lumenApi.ts` by `scripts/plugin-api-docs.mjs`; every example on it runs in the test suite. A plugin asks for apiVersion 1 in its manifest. For events, limits and UI elements see [Plugin API](/plugins/api/).

## `lumen.on`

```ts illustrative
on(event: string, handler: (payload: unknown) => void): () => void
```

Listen to an event: `command:<id>`, `render:<lang>`, `ui:panel`, `ui:block`, `panel:closed`. Returns the function that stops listening. Each call of your handler gets 250 ms of CPU.

- Capability: `—`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
const off = lumen.on("panel:closed", () => console.log("closed"));
off();
```

## `lumen.manifest`

```ts illustrative
readonly manifest: { id: string; name: string; version: string; [field: string]: unknown }
```

Your manifest, read-only.

- Capability: `—`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
console.log(lumen.manifest.id, lumen.manifest.version);
```

## `lumen.document.getText`

```ts illustrative
getText(): Promise<string>
```

The open note's whole Markdown text.

- Capability: `document:read`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
const text = await lumen.document.getText();
console.log(text.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length, "words");
```

## `lumen.document.getFileName`

```ts illustrative
getFileName(): Promise<string>
```

The open note's file name (`notes/plan.md`), or `Untitled.md`.

- Capability: `document:read`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
const name = await lumen.document.getFileName();
console.log(name.endsWith(".md"));
```

## `lumen.document.getSelection`

```ts illustrative
getSelection(): Promise<{ from: number; to: number; text: string } | null>
```

The selection: `{ from, to, text }`, or `null` when nothing is selected.

- Capability: `document:read`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
const sel = await lumen.document.getSelection();
if (sel) console.log(sel.text.length, "characters selected");
```

## `lumen.document.setText`

```ts illustrative
setText(text: string): Promise<void>
```

Replace the open note's whole text (one undo step). It loses the cursor, the selection and the user's undo steps.

- Capability: `document:write`
- Since apiVersion: 1
- **Deprecated:** use document.applyEdits (apiVersion 1.1) — removed in apiVersion 2

```js illustrative
const text = await lumen.document.getText();
await lumen.document.setText(text.replace(/\s+$/g, "") + "\n");
```

## `lumen.document.insertText`

```ts illustrative
insertText(text: string): Promise<void>
```

Insert text at the cursor (it replaces a selection).

- Capability: `document:write`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
await lumen.document.insertText(`\n> נכתב ב-${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}\n`);
```

## `lumen.document.replaceSelection`

```ts illustrative
replaceSelection(text: string): Promise<void>
```

Replace the selected text.

- Capability: `document:write`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
const sel = await lumen.document.getSelection();
if (sel) await lumen.document.replaceSelection(sel.text.toUpperCase());
```

## `lumen.document.applyEdits`

```ts illustrative
applyEdits(edits: { from: number; to: number; insert: string }[]): Promise<number>
```

Replacements `{ from, to, insert }`, in the coordinates of the text before the batch, applied as one undoable change; resolves to how many were applied (W13.L1).

- Capability: `document:write`
- Since apiVersion: 1.1

```js illustrative
const text = await lumen.document.getText();
const at = text.indexOf("world");
if (at >= 0) await lumen.document.applyEdits([{ from: at, to: at + 5, insert: "עולם" }]);
```

## `lumen.vault.list`

```ts illustrative
list(dir?: string): Promise>
```

The vault's entries under `dir` (relative, no `..`, no hidden folders).

- Capability: `vault:read`
- Since apiVersion: 1

```js illustrative
const entries = await lumen.vault.list("notes");
console.log(entries.filter((e) => e.path.endsWith(".md")).length);
```

## `lumen.vault.read`

```ts illustrative
read(path: string): Promise<string>
```

A file's text (5 MB at most).

pages.title: Plugin API
pages.description: The lumen object a sandboxed plugin gets — every method, the capability it needs, its limits, and the UI elements.
pages.md:
A plugin's `main` is an ES module that runs in the sandbox (see
[Sandbox and permissions](/plugins/sandbox/)). It talks to Lumen only
through the global `lumen` object. Every method returns a promise. A
method whose capability you were not granted rejects with a `PluginDenied`
error.

## Events

```js
const off = lumen.on(name, (payload) => { … }); // off() unsubscribes
```

| Event | When | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `command:<id>` | One of your commands ran | `{ source: "palette" }` |
| `render:<lang>` | A ```` ```<lang> ```` block needs rendering | `{ requestId, source }` |
| `ui:panel` / `ui:block` | A button was clicked or a field changed in your panel / block | `{ id, kind: "click" \| "change", value? }` |
| `panel:closed` | The user closed your panel | — |

Your handlers get 250 ms of CPU each time they are called. Waiting for a
`lumen.*` call does not count toward that.

## Methods

| Method | Capability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `document.getText()` / `getFileName()` / `getSelection()` | `document:read` | `getSelection()` → `{ from, to, text }` or `null` |
| `document.setText(text)` / `insertText(text)` / `replaceSelection(text)` | `document:write` | Insert replaces the selection at the cursor |
| `vault.list(dir?)` / `vault.read(path)` | `vault:read` | Relative paths only: no `..` and no hidden folders. Reads are capped at 5 MB |
| `vault.write(path, text)` | `vault:write` | `.md`, `.txt`, `.json` or `.csv` only, 5 MB at most |
| `commands.register({ id, label, hint? }, handler?)` / `commands.unregister(id)` | `commands` | Up to 50 per plugin. The label shows "· your plugin name" |
| `panel.open({ title? })` / `panel.render(tree)` / `panel.close()` | `panel` | One plugin panel at a time |
| `renderer.register(lang)` / `renderer.result(requestId, tree)` | `renderer` | Up to 10 languages. Languages Lumen renders itself (`mermaid`, `chart`, `csv`, …) are refused |
| `settings.get()` / `settings.set(object)` | `settings` | Your own JSON, 64 KB at most |
| `storage.get(key)` / `set(key, value)` / `delete(key)` | `storage` | Your own key–value store: 1,000 keys of at most 1 MB each. Removed when you are uninstalled |
| `clipboard.writeText(text)` | `clipboard:write` | — |
| `notifications.show(text, "info" \| "success" \| "error")` | `notifications` | Shown with your name in front |
| `network.fetch(url, { method?, headers?, body? })` | `network:<origin>` | Only to the exact origin you were granted. No cookies, no redirects, 30 s timeout, 5 MB at most. Returns `{ status, headers, body }`. Recorded in the privacy ledger; blocked under local-only |
| `bases.query(path, view?, { offset?, limit? })` | `bases:read` | A `.base` view's rows, as the app shows them: `{ view, columns, rows: [{ path, cells }], total, errors }`. Cells are JSON (dates as ISO text, links as paths). At most 10,000 rows per call |
| `bases.update([{ path, set: { property: value } }])` | `bases:write` | Changes note properties. **One approval screen covers the whole call**: the user sees how many notes, which properties and the first five, and nothing is written unless they allow it. At most 5,000 rows. Returns `{ written, unchanged, declined }` |
| `lumen.manifest` | — | Your manifest (read-only) |

`console.log` / `warn` / `error` are allowed, up to 120 lines a minute.

## UI elements

Panels and rendered blocks are **trees of these elements**, and nothing
else:

`text {text}` · `heading {level 1–3, text}` · `paragraph {children}` ·
`box {direction "row"|"column", gap, children}` · `list {ordered, items: [[…]]}` ·
`button {id, label, primary?, disabled?}` · `input {id, value?, placeholder?, multiline?}` ·
`checkbox {id, label, checked?}` · `select {id, value?, options: [{value, label}]}` ·
`code {text, lang?}` · `noteLink {target, label?}` (a note in the vault, never a URL) · `divider`

A tree can have at most 2,000 nodes, nest at most 24 levels deep, and hold
at most 20,000 characters of text per node. An unknown element or field is
refused.

## Examples

The examples live in `public/plugins/examples/`:

- `word-stats` — a command, a panel, settings, `document:read`
- `callout` — a code-block renderer that keeps checklist ticks in `storage`

pages.title: Developing a plugin
pages.description: Scaffold a sandboxed plugin with create-lumen-plugin, run it with hot reload in developer mode, test it in Node with the test kit, and see what it does in the Developer panel.
pages.md:
## Five minutes from nothing to a running plugin

```bash
npx create-lumen-plugin my-plugin
cd my-plugin
npm run dev        # http://127.0.0.1:5199, watches the folder
```

1. In Lumen open **Plugin gallery**, then **Developer mode** at the bottom.
   Keep `http://127.0.0.1:5199` and press **Connect**.
2. Run the command your plugin registers from `⌘K` (in the template: *My plugin*): the side panel shows the word count of the note.
3. Change `main.js` and save. Lumen reloads the plugin by itself, usually
   in well under a second. The panel shows how long the last reload took.

Nothing needs installing: the dev server and the test kit use only Node
(20 or later).

## What is in the folder

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `lumen-plugin.json` | The manifest: id, name, version, and the capabilities the plugin asks for, each with the reason the user sees. |
| `main.js` | The plugin. It runs in the [sandbox](/plugins/sandbox/): only the `lumen` API, no DOM, no network unless asked for. |
| `test/main.test.mjs` | Tests, run with `npm test`. |
| `tools/dev-server.mjs` | The dev server behind `npm run dev`. |
| `tools/testkit.mjs` | The test kit. |

## Developer mode

Developer mode loads the plugin from the dev server instead of the
gallery:

- It connects only to this computer (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`).
- Keep the dev server on port 5199: the app's content security policy
  allows that port on this computer and no other.
- The plugin gets the capabilities its manifest asks for, without the
  permission screen: it is your own code.
- Each version is still run through the [safety scan](/plugins/permissions/),
  and the panel shows its notes. The scan's verdict does not block your own
  plugin here, but the gallery will not list a version that fails.
- On every save the dev server sends a `change` event and Lumen loads the
  manifest and `main.js` again. Changes that arrive during a reload are
  collected into one more reload.

## The Developer panel

While the plugin runs, the panel shows:

- **Reloads**: how many, how long the last one took (from the save to the
  plugin running again), and how long the start took.
- **CPU and memory**: the time spent in the plugin's code, how many runs,
  the longest, and the sandbox's memory.
- **Permissions: asked for and used**: each capability in the manifest,
  how often it was used and refused. A capability that is never used is
  marked: ask only for what you use, because users see the list before
  they install.
- **Last calls**: the plugin's last calls to Lumen, with their time and
  whether they were refused.

## Testing in Node

```js




test("shows the count", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", document: { text: "שלום עולם" } });
  await p.run("show");                       // a command it registered
  assert.equal(p.panel.tree.type, "box");    // the panel it rendered
});

test("needs document:read", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", grants: ["commands", "panel"] });
  await assert.rejects(p.run("show"), { name: "PluginDenied" });
});
```

`loadPlugin` runs `main.js` in a fresh Node `vm` context with a mock of the
`lumen` API. It follows the sandbox's rules: the same method table (a test
in Lumen keeps the two equal), a call without its capability rejects with
`PluginDenied`, and arguments must be JSON. The mock state is `document`
(`text`, `fileName`, `selection`), `vault` (`{"folder/note.md": text}`),
`settings`, `storage` and `fetch` for granted network calls.

You get back what the plugin did: `commands`, `panel`, `rendered`,
`document`, `vault`, `storage`, `notifications`, `clipboard`, `logs`,
`calls` and `denied`. You drive it with `run(id, payload)`,
`emit(name, payload)` (for example `"ui:panel"`), `render(lang, source)`
for a code-block renderer, and `select(from, to)`.

Node is not QuickJS, so test in Lumen too before you publish. Two
differences to keep in mind: QuickJS has no `Intl`, and the sandbox
limits CPU time and memory.

## Examples

The gallery's eight examples are in `public/plugins/examples/`:

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| Word stats | A panel, settings, Hebrew and English counting |
| Callout cards | A code-block renderer, storage |
| Quote of the day | Network access to one origin |
| Table of contents | Reading and writing the note |
| Hebrew date | A renderer and a command, a calendar computed without `Intl` |
| Tasks overview | Reading the whole vault (`vault:read`), a panel with note links |
| Bidi cleaner | Selection or whole note, notifications |
| Text format | A port of an Obsidian plugin (MIT), several commands |

## Publishing

Bump `version` in `lumen-plugin.json` and open a pull request that adds
the folder under `public/plugins/examples/` and a line in its
`index.json`. Run `node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` first: every version is
scanned, and a version that fails is not listed.

The mock state is document (text, fileName, selection), vault ({"folder/note.md": text}), settings, storage and fetch for granted network calls. You get back what the plugin did: commands, panel, rendered, document, vault, storage, notifications, clipboard, logs, calls and denied. You drive it with run(id, payload), emit(name, payload) (for example "ui:panel"), render(lang, source) for a code-block renderer, and select(from, to). Node is not QuickJS, so test in Lumen too before you publish. Two differences to keep in mind: QuickJS has no Intl, and the sandbox limits CPU time and memory.

pages.md:
A sandboxed plugin can do nothing until you allow it — see the
[plugin API](/plugins/api/). Two things make that choice informed.

## The install screen

**Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…** opens a screen that lists,
before anything runs, every permission the plugin's manifest asks for:

| Permission | What it lets the plugin do |
|---|---|
| `document:read` | Read the note that is open |
| `document:write` | Change the note that is open (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:read` | Read any note in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:write` | Create and change notes in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `commands` | Add commands to the command palette |
| `panel` | Show a side panel |
| `renderer` | Draw code blocks of its own language in the preview |
| `settings` | Keep its own settings |
| `storage` | Store its own data on this device |
| `clipboard:write` | Copy text to your clipboard (*sensitive*) |
| `notifications` | Show notifications |
| `network:<origin>` | Connect to that one address — and nowhere else (*sensitive*) |

Each line also shows the plugin's own reason (“Why: …”) and the version's
safety scan. **Install and allow** grants exactly what is listed; anything
else the plugin tries is refused by the sandbox, and every network request
appears in the privacy ledger. The code is scanned again right before it
runs, so the card can't describe a different copy.

## The safety scan

Every version in the registry (`public/plugins/examples/index.json`) is
scanned by `scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` into `scan.json`; the gallery shows
each version's card — a grade (A, B, C), a score out of 100, and what the
scan noted. **A version that fails is not shown and cannot be installed.**

The scan reads the code — it never runs it — and fails a version that:

- uses an API whose permission the manifest does not declare (for example
  writes to the note with only `document:read`);
- reaches the network without declaring it, or connects to an origin other
  than the one declared;
- runs code made from text (`eval`, `Function`, string timers), loads more
  code (`import`), or indexes `globalThis` / `lumen` with a computed key;
- is not valid JavaScript, is larger than 512 KB, or has a signature that
  does not verify.

It notes (and lowers the score for) permissions asked for but not used,
indirect use of the API, network addresses built while running, and a
missing or unknown signature.

To check a new version before publishing: add it to `index.json`, then
`node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` (or `--check` to only verify).

## Reporting a problem

Every card and install screen has **Report a problem**, which opens an issue
with the plugin's id and version filled in.

pages.title: Plugin registry and the built-in ten
pages.description: The ten plugins in Lumen's plugin gallery, what each one may do, and how the static registry is built and scanned.
pages.md:
The **Sandboxed plugins** section of the Plugin Gallery lists plugins from a
static registry that ships with Lumen. There is no plugin server: the registry
is a folder of files, and every version in it passes the safety scan before it
is listed.

## The ten plugins

These are modelled on the kinds of Obsidian plugins people download most
(templates, task boards, calendars, tables, linting, tags, spaced repetition,
refactoring, dates, sorting). Each is written for Lumen's sandbox: none of them
uses the network, so they all work under the **local-only** AI policy.

| Plugin | What it does | Permissions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Templates** | Inserts a note from your `Templates` folder, filling `{{date}}`, `{{date:DD/MM/YYYY}}`, `{{time}}`, `{{title}}`, `{{selection}}`, `{{weekday}}` and `{{hebrewWeekday}}`. | commands, read the vault, read and change the open note, panel, settings |
| **Kanban board** | Draws a ` ```kanban ` block (a `## heading` per column, a `- item` per card) as columns, and copies the board as a Markdown table. | code-block renderer, commands, read and change the open note, clipboard, notifications |
| **Calendar** | A month view of your daily notes (`YYYY-MM-DD.md`). Days that have a note link to it. The week starts on Sunday, or on Monday if you choose. | commands, panel, read the vault, settings |
| **Table formatter** | Lines up the columns of every table and sorts a table by the column under the cursor. Hebrew niqqud takes no width. | commands, read and change the open note |
| **Markdown tidy** | Fixes trailing spaces, extra blank lines, heading spacing, mixed bullets and a missing final newline. It never touches code or front matter. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Tag manager** | Lists every `#tag` in the vault, Hebrew tags included, and renames a tag and its nested tags everywhere at once. | commands, panel, read and change the vault, notifications |
| **Flashcards** | Turns `question :: answer` lines into cards and schedules reviews with SM-2. The note itself is never changed. | commands, read the open note, panel, storage |
| **Note refactor** | Moves the selection into a new note and leaves a `[[link]]` in its place, or splits a note into one note per heading. | commands, read and change the open note, read and change the vault, notifications, settings |
| **Natural dates** | Turns “tomorrow”, “next Friday”, “in 3 days”, “מחר”, “יום שישי הבא” or 12/11/2026 (day first) into `[[2026-11-13]]`. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Sort lines** | Sorts the selected lines A→Z, Z→A or by length, reverses them, or removes duplicates. Sub-items stay with their item. Hebrew sorts by letter (final letters sort with their regular forms), and numbers sort by value. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications |

Install one from **Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…**. The
permission screen lists everything the plugin asks for and why. Once a plugin is
installed, its card shows **Remove**, which stops the plugin and deletes the
settings and data it stored.

The plugins write their labels in English and Hebrew, because the plugin API
does not tell a plugin which language the app is in.

## How the registry is built

```
public/plugins/examples/
  index.json          ← built: every plugin, its versions, the SHA-256 of each version's code and manifest
  index.json.sig      ← the owner's Ed25519 signature over index.json (written by --sign)
  scan.json           ← built: the safety scan of every version
  kanban/             ← one folder per version
    lumen-plugin.json
    main.js
```

```sh
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs           # rebuild index.json and scan.json
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --check   # fail if either is out of date, a version fails, or index.json.sig no longer matches
```

The build does the following:

- validates every manifest;
- refuses stray files in a plugin folder (only the manifest, its entries, a `LICENSE` and a `README` are allowed);
- refuses an id and version that appear twice;
- writes `index.json`;
- scans every version (`scripts/scan-plugins.mjs`).

A new version goes in a folder of its own, for example `kanban@1.1.0`.

When you install a plugin, the app scans the downloaded code again. It refuses
the code if its SHA-256 differs from the hash in the registry scan.

Check that the registry is current (this example runs in the docs check):

```sh run
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --check
```

## The signed registry

The owner signs the exact bytes of `index.json` with an Ed25519 key that stays
on the owner's machine. Because `index.json` lists the SHA-256 of every
version's code and manifest, that one signature covers every file a user can
install.

```sh
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --keygen ~/keys      # once: a new key; prints the VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS value
LUMEN_PLUGIN_SIGNING_KEY=~/keys/lumen-plugin-registry.pem node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --sign
```

Set the printed `VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS` in the build's environment. The app
trusts only that key, or a key you trusted yourself under Settings. The public
key written in `index.json.sig` is never trusted on its own.

When a folder has `index.json.sig`, **Install** takes the signed path
(`src/plugins/install.ts`), and each step can refuse the install:

1. `index.json` and `index.json.sig` are downloaded. The downloads are listed
   in the privacy ledger.
2. The signature over `index.json` must verify against a trusted key. One
   changed byte anywhere in `index.json` fails here.
3. The manifest and the code are downloaded, and each SHA-256 must match the
   signed `index.json`.
4. The code is scanned. Then it runs in its QuickJS sandbox with the
   permissions the manifest declares, as listed on the permission screen.

**Remove** stops the sandbox, deletes what the plugin stored and deletes its
install record and permissions.

A registry from another site is installed only through this path, and an
unsigned one is refused. Only the folder that ships with the app
(`/plugins/examples`), served from the app's own origin, falls back to the
SHA-256 check against its scan when it has no `index.json.sig`.

## Themes tested in RTL (W12.S6)

Every theme in the gallery (`public/themes/examples/`) is reviewed like a
plugin version with only a stylesheet (the review on the
[Security](/security/) page: licence, public source, no remote CSS), and then
checked for right-to-left use. `node scripts/themes/rtl-check.mjs` writes its
scorecard to `public/themes/examples/scorecards/<id>@<version>.json`;
`--check` fails when one is stale, and `--css <file>` checks one stylesheet.

- **Physical CSS.** `margin-left`, `padding-right`, `left:`/`right:`,
  one-sided borders and corners, `float`, `clear` and `text-align` with
  `left`/`right` break a Hebrew layout. Each one is reported with the
  logical property to use instead (`margin-inline-start`, `text-align:
  start`, …). A rule scoped to one direction (`[dir="rtl"] …`, `:dir(ltr)`)
  is allowed.
- **Contrast** (WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3): the theme's text colours against its
  backgrounds, 4.5:1, in light and in dark. The app's own colours fill in
  whatever the theme leaves unset.
- **Screens.** Eight screens (editor, preview, table, lists, callouts, code
  inside Hebrew, Bases, settings) are captured in RTL and in LTR by a
  browser run, merged with `--screens <results.json>`.

A failing RTL check is a warning on the scorecard, not a delisting: each
finding costs the score what any review warning costs (10 points). The
**Tested in RTL** badge is given only when all three pass, so it waits for
the browser run. There are no user ratings: ratings need accounts and
moderation, and the scorecard and the badge do that job.

## A registry site of its own

The same registry can be published as a static site of its own on Cloudflare
Pages, the second host. A developer outside the project can then get a plugin
listed with a pull request, without waiting for an app release.

```sh
npm run registry:site                 # builds dist-registry/ (it first checks that index.json and scan.json are current)
npm run registry:verify -- dist-registry
npx wrangler pages deploy dist-registry --project-name lumen-md-plugins --branch main
npm run registry:verify -- https://lumen-md-plugins.pages.dev
```

The site holds:

- `v1/index.json`: every plugin and every version that passed its scan, with
  its permissions, its scan grade and findings, and the SHA-256 and size of
  each file. A version that failed its scan is left out.
- `v1/plugins/<id>/<version>/`: the files. They are served as text and never
  rewritten, so they can be cached forever.
- `SHA256SUMS`, in the format `sha256sum -c` reads.
- `index.html`: the list, in Hebrew and English, with no scripts.
- `_headers`: `nosniff`, read-only CORS, and a CSP that allows nothing to run.

`registry:verify` recomputes every hash and **scans every version again**
on your machine. A host that changed a file, or that lists a version the scan
would refuse, fails the check. The site fits the free plan with room to
spare: 40 files of the 20,000 allowed, 4 header rules of the 100 allowed.

The app still reads the registry it ships (`/plugins/examples`). Reading this
site from the app is a separate step, because the app's CSP would need its
address.

## Not yet

- The registry that ships with the app is **not signed yet**: signing it needs
  the owner's key (`--keygen`, then `--sign`, above), so its cards still show
  the “unsigned” note. See also [Plugin signing keys](/plugins/signing/).
- The registry site (`npm run registry:site`) does not publish `index.json.sig`
  yet, and the app does not read that site yet.

pages.title: Plugin sandbox and permissions
pages.description: How Lumen runs plugins with no access by default — QuickJS for logic, UI as data, a capability list the user grants.
pages.md:
Lumen runs every plugin with **no access by default**. A plugin gets only
the capabilities you grant it when you install it, and you can revoke them
at any time.

## Where plugin code runs

| Part | Runs in | What it can reach |
|---|---|---|
| Logic (`main`) | [QuickJS](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten) (MIT), a separate JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly, inside its own Web Worker | Only the `lumen` object. There is no `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `importScripts`, DOM or storage, and no `import` of other modules. |
| Interface (panels, settings, block output) | Lumen itself | The plugin sends a **tree of known elements**: text, heading, paragraph, box, list, button, input, checkbox, select, code, link to a note, divider. There is no `img`, `iframe`, `form`, `style`, `script` or HTML, and no link to a web address. |

The interface is data rather than a sandboxed iframe on purpose. CSP and the
iframe `sandbox` attribute block every channel but one: a frame may always
navigate *itself* (`location = "https://…?" + text`). A tree of known
elements has no such channel.

## Limits

Each plugin has a 32 MB heap and a 512 KB stack. It gets 250 ms of CPU each
time Lumen enters its code (an event, the reply to a call), and its console
is capped at 120 lines a minute. A plugin that goes over a limit, or throws
an error nobody catches, is stopped.

## Capabilities

| Capability | Gives |
|---|---|
| `document:read` / `document:write` | The open note's text and selection / changing it |
| `vault:read` / `vault:write` | Listing and reading notes / writing notes |
| `commands` | Commands in the palette |
| `panel` | A side panel |
| `renderer` | Rendering a code-block language |
| `settings` | A settings section |
| `storage` | Its own key–value storage |
| `clipboard:write` | Copying text |
| `notifications` | Toasts |
| `network:https://exact.origin` | Requests to **that origin only** — https (http only for localhost), no cookies, no redirects, at most 5 MB of response |

Every capability the manifest asks for comes with a reason, which is shown
to you before you grant it. A call without its capability fails inside the
plugin with `PluginDenied` and never reaches Lumen. Lumen checks the grant
a second time on the host side, because the worker is a boundary, not the
policy.

## Network and privacy

Every request a plugin makes appears in the **privacy ledger** under
"Plugin". Under the **local-only** AI policy, plugin requests are blocked
and logged as blocked, even when the plugin has a network grant.

## Manifest (`lumen-plugin.json`)

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "org.example.word-stats",
  "name": "Word stats",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Counts words in the open note",
  "author": "Example",
  "license": "MIT",
  "main": "main.js",
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "document:read", "reason": "To count the words of the open note" },
    { "id": "commands", "reason": "Adds the “Word stats” command" }
  ]
}
```

sections.text: Capability Gives --- --- document:read / document:write The open note's text and selection / changing it vault:read / vault:write Listing and reading notes / writing notes commands Commands in the palette panel A side panel renderer Rendering a code-block language settings A settings section storage Its own key–value storage clipboard:write Copying text notifications Toasts network:https://exact.origin Requests to that origin only — https (http only for localhost), no cookies, no redirects, at most 5 MB of response Every capability the manifest asks for comes with a reason, which is shown to you before you grant it. A call without its capability fails inside the plugin with PluginDenied and never reaches Lumen. Lumen checks the grant a second time on the host side, because the worker is a boundary, not the policy.

sections.heading: Network and privacy
sections.text: Every request a plugin makes appears in the privacy ledger under "Plugin". Under the local-only AI policy, plugin requests are blocked and logged as blocked, even when the plugin has a network grant.
